newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania concerned over pace of Italian-led force.
newsitem.headline: Albania concerned over pace of Italian-led force.

text.p: Albania expressed concern on Monday about the slowness of deployment of an Italian-led force to protect aid to the anarchic state as Rome faced political turmoil over sending troops.
"There is a little concern" (about the pace of deployment), Foreign Minister Arjan Starova told Reuters. "We'd like a speedy action...we want this force as soon as possible."

"But I have no doubt they will come," Starova said of the force of up to 6,000 troops. Italy has said the force, approved by the U.N. Security Council on March 28, will start arriving in the week starting April 14.

In Rome, a hard-left ally of Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi reaffirmed it would vote against sending Italian troops, splitting Prodi's parliamentary majority on a major policy issue for the first time.

Despite opposition of the Communist Refoundation party, Prodi is certain of victory when the two houses of parliament hold votes on the force on Tuesday and Wednesday because of backing for the deployment from the main opposition.
U.N. relief agencies have warned that about 400,000 people may be threatened by hunger after an armed uprising last month pushed Albania close to chaos.

In new violence, three people were killed at the weekend in gun battles around the southern port of Vlore, held by rebels after last month's armed uprising sparked by anger over the collapse of popular savings schemes.
Four children in the town were injured playing with detonators. One six-year-old boy had his hand amputated, doctors said.

Mourners in the central village of Levan held funerals on Monday for two sisters, Dituri and Vjollca Kacupi, who drowned in the Adriatic after a collision between their refugee boat and an Italian corvette on March 28.

Only four bodies were recovered after the sinking and the girls' funeral has become a new focus of grief. Tirana says at least 80 people died and 34 survived. Another man who drowned was buried in Fier on Sunday.

Starova said states taking part in the planned force were still debating where they would deploy troops. The forces plan to secure the northern port of Durres, Vlore in the rebel-held south and Tirana airport.
"There are certain problems around the deployment of forces, the areas where this force or that force belonging to this country or that country will be deployed," he said.
"I think they will find a consensus," he said. Greece has publicly said it is at odds with Italy over deployment.

A few dozen people laid flowers on a monument in the northern port of Durres on Monday to commemorate the 58th anniversary of the invasion Albania by Italian troops under fascist leader Benito Mussolini on April 7, 1939.
For many Albanians, scarred by a Stalinist dictatorship for almost 45 years after the war, the anniversary has little significance.
Tirana was also searching for toxic chemicals and radioactive materials, some of them used in radar, that it said were stolen from four military arsenals last month.
"They can kill...please hand them back," Colonel Asllan Bushati told Albanian television on Sunday.
Starova said he agreed with U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who called for the rapid deployment of the Italian-led force. "Speed is of the essence," Annan said in New Delhi.
Italian Prime Minister Prodi was due to visit Vlore -- both the port from which the refugee boat left and a port the Italian-led force is meant to secure -- in coming days.
Italy is expected to provide between 2,000 and 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. Austria and Denmark say they are also considering participation.
